safetyNote: Histoplasma capsulatum is a pathogenic dimorphic fungus. Its environmental conidia can be infectious when inhaled, and sporulating cultures pose a serious occupational hazard. This plate is an educational illustration, not an invitation to collect, culture, or handle the fungus. Identification belongs to specialized diagnostic methods.

sections.title: A dimorphic fungus
sections.text: Histoplasma capsulatum changes form with its environment. In nature it grows as a filamentous mould; in tissues at body temperature it takes a yeast form. This plate compares those two morphologies and does not depict a mushroom with a cap and stem.

sections.title: Mycelial phase and conidia
sections.text: The mould forms hyaline, septate, branching hyphae. They bear small, smooth microconidia, usually oval to pyriform and about 2–4 µm, and larger globose, thick-walled macroconidia, about 7–15 µm, with characteristic tuberculate projections. Microconidia are the environmental propagules chiefly associated with infection by inhalation.

sections.title: Tissue yeast phase
sections.text: In tissue, cells are small oval yeasts, generally about 2–4 µm, with narrow-based budding. They are often seen inside macrophages, but may also occur extracellularly. A clear halo around a cell in a tissue section can give the impression of a capsule; H. capsulatum does not have a true capsule.

sections.title: Ecology and diagnosis
sections.text: Histoplasma occurs in several regions of the world and lives in soil. Soil or material enriched with bird or bat droppings can support its growth, but these droppings are not required for its presence. Conidia may become airborne when contaminated material is disturbed. Tuberculate macroconidia are suggestive, but are not sufficient by themselves to confirm the species; morphology must be interpreted by a specialist laboratory and supplemented as appropriate.

sections.title: Reading the plate
sections.text: On the left, the mycelial phase shows septate hyphae bearing smooth microconidia and large, rounded macroconidia with tuberculate projections. On the right, the tissue phase shows oval, narrow-budding yeasts, some within a macrophage. These are schematic microscopic views at different scales; no macroscopic fruit body is expected.

traits: Pathogenic microscopic dimorphic fungus, with no cap-and-stem fruit body.
Mycelial phase: hyaline, septate and branching hyphae.
Globose, thick-walled, tuberculate macroconidia, about 7–15 µm.
Tissue phase: oval yeasts about 2–4 µm, with narrow-based budding, often intracellular in macrophages.
Inhaled conidia can cause infection; morphology alone cannot confirm identification.
